summary.title: Spectro-temporal study of atoll source GX 9+9 observed with AstroSat
summary.authors: Sree Bhattacherjee, Arbind Pradhan, Biplob Sarkar
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) GX 9+9 using data from the AstroSat mission. The source, identified as an atoll source, was observed in the soft/banana state during a single archival observation on July 25, 2020. The analysis utilized the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) instruments to cover a broad energy range of 0.7–25.0 keV. The spectral analysis employed a simultaneous fitting approach using the model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), which provided a good fit to the data across three distinct flux levels (FL1, FL2, FL3). The results indicate a disk-dominated energy spectrum, with the inner disk radius estimated at approximately 16.57±1.29 km. The total unabsorbed flux increased from FL1 to FL3, reaching a maximum of 7.30×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻². Temporal analysis of the LAXPC data revealed broad-band noise (BBN) features without significant quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). The power density spectrum was fitted with two Lorentzian components, with a characteristic frequency of ~0.1 Hz. Using the propagative model formalized by Garg et al., the study attributed the variability to changes in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering, with a positive phase lag indicating the propagation of perturbations from the disk to the corona. The findings suggest the source is transitioning towards a softer state, characterized by a decrease in Comptonization temperature and an increase in disk temperature. The study highlights the utility of AstroSat's wide energy coverage and high timing resolution in characterizing poorly studied sources like GX 9+9, though limitations due to poor data quality and single-observation constraints are noted.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) GX 9+9 using data from the AstroSat mission. The source, identified as an atoll source, was observed in the soft/banana state during a single archival observation on July 25, 2020. The analysis utilized the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) instruments to cover a broad energy range of 0.7–25.0 keV. The spectral analysis employed a simultaneous fitting approach using the model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), which provided a good fit to the data across three distinct flux levels (FL1, FL2, FL3). The results indicate a disk-dominated energy spectrum, with the inner disk radius estimated at approximately 16.57±1.29 km. The total unabsorbed flux increased from FL1 to FL3, reaching a maximum of 7.30×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻². Temporal analysis of the LAXPC data revealed broad-band noise (BBN) features without significant quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). The power density spectrum was fitted with two Lorentzian components, with a characteristic frequency of ~0.1 Hz. Using the propagative model formalized by Garg et al., the study attributed the variability to changes in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering, with a positive phase lag indicating the propagation of perturbations from the disk to the corona. The findings suggest the source is transitioning towards a softer state, characterized by a decrease in Comptonization temperature and an increase in disk temperature. The study highlights the utility of AstroSat's wide energy coverage and high timing resolution in characterizing poorly studied sources like GX 9+9, though limitations due to poor data quality and single-observation constraints are noted.

Research Context
GX 9+9 is a neutron star low-mass X-ray binary identified during a rocket mission. It is an established atoll source tracing a 'C'-pattern in the hardness-intensity diagram. Atoll sources have hard/island and soft/banana states with distinct spectral characteristics. The source exhibits 4.2-hour modulation in X-ray and optical wavebands. Previous studies used various spectral models including power laws and blackbodies. Recent work emphasized spectral modeling for coronal plasma understanding. AstroSat offers larger effective area and wider energy coverage than RXTE. The source is not well-studied, necessitating estimation of basic characteristics.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to investigate the spectro-temporal properties of GX 9+9 using AstroSat data. It seeks to compare the constancy between spectral and temporal analyses. The goal includes estimating source characteristics like inner-disk radius and flux. The hypothesis is that the source is in the soft state with disk-dominated emission. It is hypothesized that variability originates from radiative mechanisms in the disk-corona system. The study predicts that spectral parameters will vary with increasing X-ray flux. It is expected that the source is transitioning towards a softer state. The temporal analysis aims to identify the origin of observed variability.

Methodological Details
Data was obtained from a single AstroSat archival observation on July 25, 2020. The LAXPC and SXT instruments were used for spectral analysis. Only LAXPC data was used for timing due to high timing resolution. LAXPC 20 data was used as counters 10 and 30 suffered abnormal gains. LAXPC operates over a wide energy band from 3-80 keV. SXT works in the low energy range of 0.3-8.0 keV. Good time interval data was extracted using the standard LAXPC software pipeline. SXT data was processed using the AS1SXTLevel2-1.4b pipeline. An annular zone was used to limit SXT counts below the pileup threshold. A 2% model systematic error was incorporated for background uncertainty. Spectra were grouped using the ftool ftgrouppha. Spectral analysis was performed in the energy range of 0.7–25 keV. The XSPEC package of HEASOFT was used for spectral fitting. The source was segregated into three distinct flux levels for analysis. FL1, FL2, and FL3 correspond to specific count rate ranges.

Procedures And Architectures
The best-fit spectral model was const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb). The thermal Comptonization model ThComp was used as an improved version. A cross-calibration component 'const' was incorporated for joint fitting. The LAXPC 20 constant was fixed at 1, leaving SXT free. The optical depth was frozen at 9 to constrain other parameters. Edge models at 2.4 keV were required for a better fit. The inner-disk radius was calculated using a specific relation involving k and Ndbb. The color-correction factor k was set to 1.7. The disk inclination angle was considered as 60 degrees. The source distance was assumed to be 10 kpc. The total unabsorbed flux was estimated using the XSPEC model 'cflux'. The power density spectrum was fitted with a multi-lorentzian approach. Two Lorentzians were required to fit the PDS. The characteristic frequency was calculated using the centroid frequency and HWHM. The propagative model by Garg et al. was used for temporal modeling. The model relates spectral parameters with physical parameters.

Key Results
The source was detected in the soft state during the observation. The average inner-disk radius was estimated to be ~16.57±1.29 km. The total unabsorbed flux in FL1 was ~5.94×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻². The total unabsorbed flux in FL2 was ~6.51×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻². The total unabsorbed flux in FL3 was ~7.30×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻². No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected in discrete flux levels. A BBN-like feature was observed in the full flux PDS. The centroid frequency of the BBN feature was ~0.04 Hz. The characteristic frequency was ~0.1 Hz. The rms increased with energy while phase lag decreased. The reduced χ² value for the temporal model was ~0.80. The variation in kTin was 0.56 ± 0.10%. The variation in fs was 81 ± 32%. The phase lag was 0.11 ± 0.08. The source is suggested to be transitioning towards a softer state.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The disk-dominated spectrum suggests thermal emission from the accretion disk. The increase in flux from FL1 to FL3 indicates higher accretion rates. The estimated inner-disk radius is consistent with previous reports. The decrease in kTe and increase in Tin suggest a transition to a softer state. The BBN variability is attributed to changes in inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering. The positive phase lag indicates propagation from the disk to the corona. The results support the propagative model for explaining stochastic variability. The study highlights the importance of wide energy coverage for spectral modeling.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is constrained by poor data quality of the source. GX 9+9 is not a well-studied source, limiting comparative analysis. Only a single archival observation was available for this study. The phase lag errors are consistent within data points, limiting reliability. Further research with multiple mission observations is necessary. The distance and inclination angle assumptions may affect radius estimates. The lack of QPOs limits the application of certain timing models.

Claims
The source GX 9+9 is in the soft state with a disk-dominated spectrum. The source was detected in the soft state. The spectrum is disk-dominated within 0.7–25.0 keV. Previous studies used various models including power laws. This supports the atoll source classification.
The inner-disk radius is approximately 16.57 km. The estimated Rin is ~16.57±1.29 km. This is consistent with previous estimates. Previous estimates used different distance and inclination assumptions. This provides a constraint on the compact object size.
The variability is caused by changes in inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering. The temporal model fits the rms and lag spectra. The phase lag is positive, indicating disk-to-corona propagation. The phase lag errors are large. This supports the propagative model for BBN.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The blackbody surface model failed with reduced χ² > 2. The diskbb model provided a good fit. Adding heating rate and optical depth combinations gave insignificant χ². The best-fit model varied kTin and fs with time delay.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the HID of the source with different flux levels. Figure 2 displays the best-fit spectra for FL1, FL2, and FL3. Figure 3 shows the PDS fit and energy-dependent temporal modeling. Table 1 lists the best-fit parameters for spectral and temporal analysis.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the spectro-temporal characterization of GX 9+9 using AstroSat. 2. The strongest evidence is the successful fitting of BBN variability using the propagative model. 3. The future path involves further research with multiple mission observations.
